passage:
“Akash, you getting the cheese sandwich and the shake again?” Gargi asked, holding her tray.
“Everyone's getting it. It would look weird if I just had a samosa.”
“That's about a hundred a day.”
“I know. It's the 28th.” He stared into his wallet. “I've got 140 rupees left for the rest of the month.”
“What were you saving for?”
“A proper football. I wanted it by now.”
“And?”
“Not even close.” He put the shake back in the fridge. “Maybe I'll have the samosa. What will they say?”
“I think Manav only buys it because Dev does. Everyone's copying someone.”
Akash laughed, a little embarrassed. “Okay. Samosa and tea. If they laugh, I'll survive.”

qa.q: How much money does Akash have left for the rest of the month?
qa.a: Akash has 140 rupees left for the rest of the month.

qa.q: Why did Akash keep buying the cheese sandwich and the shake?
qa.a: He was afraid of feeling left out, since it would look weird to have only a samosa, so he wanted to fit in with his classmates.

qa.q: What could Akash try with his friends instead?
qa.a: He could set a small treat budget and still join them with something cheaper, since he can stay part of the group while protecting the football fund.

qa.q: How might Gargi see Akash's spending?
qa.a: Gargi seems concerned but friendly, since she asks what he was saving for without judging and points out that everyone is copying someone.

grounding: A student buys expensive treats to match classmates at the canteen and finds at month end that little remains for what he wanted.

passage:
In Class Nine I spent most of my allowance on things I didn't even like. I'm Dhruv, and I can explain.
My group ate lunch at the canteen, and they always ordered the expensive stuff: cold coffee, cheese sandwiches, the big chocolate bar. My tiffin from home suddenly looked babyish. So I ordered what they ordered. Cold coffee, which I don't really like. Every day.
Once Minakshi from our class said she'd rather save for the science fair kit, and one of the boys laughed, and I laughed too, though I secretly wanted that kit as well.
At the end of the month I emptied my wallet on my bed. Sixty rupees. I'd wanted a set of drawing pens for months, and now it was months away again.
The worst part was that nobody would have noticed if I'd opened my tiffin. I was paying not to feel left out, and I still felt it.

qa.q: How much was left in Dhruv's wallet at the end of the month?
Why did Dhruv order cold coffee every day?
qa.a: Dhruv felt left out and embarrassed by the home tiffin, and wanted to fit in with the group.

qa.q: What else could Dhruv have tried at the canteen?
qa.a: Open the tiffin and join the chat anyway, or buy a treat once a week, keeping money for the drawing pens.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when the boys laughed?
qa.a: Minakshi was probably hurt or embarrassed, laughed at for choosing to save for something she cared about.

grounding: Shows a student buying pricey canteen treats to match his group and finding at month end that little is left for what he actually wanted.

passage:
Parent's note, end of the month
Gautam asked me today for an advance on next month's allowance, the second time this term. When I asked what for, it turned out to be the model rocket kit he has talked about since summer. He had planned to buy it with this month's money.
We sat down and went through where the money went. Almost all of it had gone at the café near his tuition, where his friends go after class: milkshakes, fries, sometimes pizza on Fridays. He admitted he often wasn't hungry. “If I just sit there with nothing, it's weird,” he said. His cousin Binita, who goes to the same tuition, said most of them feel the same and nobody says so.
He was quiet and a bit ashamed. I did not give the advance. We agreed he would try going to the café only on Fridays and see how it feels. I will check with him at the end of next month.

qa.q: Where had most of Gautam's money gone?
qa.a: The café near his tuition: milkshakes, fries, sometimes pizza on Fridays.

qa.q: What did Gautam feel about sitting at the café with nothing?
qa.a: He felt awkward and afraid of seeming odd, which is why he kept buying things he didn't want.

qa.q: What else could Gautam try besides the café only on Fridays?
qa.a: Suggest a walk or a cheaper place to his friends some days, since Binita says others feel the same.

qa.q: How might Binita see the café habit?
qa.a: Binita sees that many of them spend out of the same quiet pressure, which nobody admits.

grounding: A parent notes a student spending his allowance at a café to match friends and finding little left for the rocket kit he actually wanted.
